opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think that's something people often underestimate. When you say "simulation," most people think of the physics engine — the thing that integrates the dynamics, handles contacts, and so on. And of course that's essential, and having a fast, GPU-based simulator was a big enabler for us. But in practice, the simulator is maybe a third of the story.

On top of it you have to build the whole environment around the task. That means defining the observations — what the robot actually gets to see, and making sure that matches what it will have on the real hardware, with the right noise, latencies, and update rates. Then there's the action space and how actions map to the actuators. For legged robots, for example, we often output joint position targets that go through a PD controller, and how you model that actuator — whether you use an analytical model or something like a learned actuator network — makes a huge difference for sim-to-real transfer.

Then there's the reward design, which is its own art. You have the main task reward, like tracking a velocity command, but then you need a whole set of regularization terms — penalizing joint torques, accelerations, foot slipping, jerky actions — so the behavior is something you'd actually want to run on a real robot and not some exploit of the simulator.

You also need domain randomization: randomizing friction, masses, motor strengths, pushing the robot, adding sensor noise, so the policy becomes robust to the mismatch between simulation and reality. And terrain generation and curriculum — you can't just throw the robot onto stairs from the beginning; you need to automatically adapt difficulty so it learns progressively.

And finally there's all the infrastructure: resets, termination conditions, running thousands of environments in parallel efficiently, logging, making it easy to iterate. A lot of the real progress came from getting all of these pieces right together, so that you can train a policy in minutes, look at it, change something, and train again. That fast iteration loop is really what makes the approach work.

r001.rationale: The response says stairs should not be introduced from the beginning and that the curriculum should adapt difficulty so the robot learns progressively, communicating a progression toward harder stair terrain.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, because I think people often conflate the two. The simulator is the physics engine, right? It's the thing that computes contacts and integrates the dynamics. That's the part people usually think about when they hear "simulation." But honestly, when we were building Isaac Gym environments for legged robots, the physics engine was maybe a third of the work, if that.

The rest is everything around it. So first there's the robot model itself. You get a URDF from a manufacturer or from a CAD export, and it's basically never right. The collision geometry is too detailed, or missing, or the inertias are wrong because someone exported them with default values. The joint limits don't match what the real actuators can do. So you spend a lot of time just cleaning that up and making sure the thing you're simulating actually resembles the robot in the lab.

Then there's the actuator modeling, which for legged robots is a huge deal. The physics engine will happily apply whatever torque you ask for, instantly. Real motors don't do that. They have delays, they have friction, they saturate, and the low-level PD controller running on the robot has its own dynamics. If you don't model that, your policy learns to exploit behavior that doesn't exist in reality. So in the ANYmal work we actually trained a small network on real actuator data to capture that, and plugged it into the simulation loop.

And then there's the whole layer that's really about the RL side rather than physics. Terrain generation, so the robot sees stairs and slopes and rough ground, with a curriculum so it doesn't just fail immediately on hard terrain. Domain randomization on masses, friction, latencies, so the policy is robust to what you got wrong in the model. Observation design, noise injection, reward shaping. Reset logic, which sounds trivial but in a massively parallel setup with thousands of environments, how and when you reset matters a lot for what the policy learns.

And then there's the plumbing. Making all of this run on the GPU without copying data back and forth, because the whole point of something like Isaac Gym is that you have thousands of robots stepping in parallel and you don't want Python loops in the middle of it. A lot of the engineering is just keeping everything as tensor operations.

So I'd say the simulator gives you the dynamics, but the environment is really where you encode your understanding of the robot and of the task. And in my experience the quality of that layer is what determines whether sim-to-real works, much more than how accurate the physics engine is in some abstract sense.

r001.rationale: The response mentions stairs and a terrain curriculum to avoid immediate failure on hard terrain, but it does not state that stair difficulty progressively increases or connect that progression specifically to traversing complex stairs.

astra-6.text:
I think the simulator is really just one piece of it. It gives you the physics: you apply torques to the joints, step forward in time, and get the next state of the robot. But you still have to define the learning problem around that. What does the policy observe? What actions can it take? What behavior do you reward? How do you initialize the robot, and when do you reset an episode?

For locomotion, for example, you also need to generate terrain and decide how to expose the robot to increasingly difficult situations. If everything is too difficult at the beginning, the robot just falls and doesn’t learn much. But if everything stays easy, it won’t learn the robustness you want.

And if you want to transfer the policy to a real robot, you have to think about what’s missing or imperfect in simulation—things like actuator behavior, delays, and uncertainty in friction or mass. So building the environment is really about putting all these pieces together so that solving the task in simulation produces behavior that is useful on the actual robot.

r001.rationale: The response mentions generating terrain and exposing a locomotion policy to increasingly difficult situations, but it does not state that the curriculum uses progressively more difficult stairs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the simulator is really just one component. It gives you the physics, but you still have to define the task that the robot is going to learn. What does the policy observe? What actions can it take? How do those actions translate into motor commands? And then, of course, how do you define the reward?

You also need to think about the conditions the robot will encounter. For a walking robot, that includes the terrain, the commands you give it, and disturbances that might push it off balance. You have to decide how to initialize episodes and when to terminate them. All of those choices influence what the policy learns.

And if you want to deploy on a real robot, you need to account for the differences between simulation and reality. So building the environment is really about putting together the whole learning problem around the physics engine, so that solving it produces behavior you actually want on the robot.

r001.rationale: The response discusses defining tasks, terrain, disturbances, and sim-to-real considerations, but does not state that stair traversal training requires a curriculum of progressively harder stairs.
